daily.title: The Migration of Monarch Butterflies
passage: A

Every autumn, millions of monarch butterflies embark on one of the most remarkable journeys in the natural world, travelling up to 4,000 kilometres from Canada and the northern United States to the forests of central Mexico. What makes this migration so extraordinary is that no single butterfly completes the round trip.
B

Scientists have long been puzzled by how the insects navigate. Recent research suggests that monarchs rely on a combination of the position of the sun and an internal magnetic compass that allows them to maintain a consistent southward bearing even on cloudy days.
C

The overwintering sites in Mexico were unknown to scientists until 1975, when a research team finally located the dense colonies clinging to oyamel fir trees at high altitude. The discovery raised urgent questions about conservation, as logging threatened the very forests the butterflies depend on.
D

Climate change now poses an additional threat. Warmer temperatures disrupt the delicate timing of migration, and unusual weather events can devastate colonies that have gathered in a single location. Only monarchs born in late summer make the migration, and it may be their great-grandchildren that return the following year.

_oldDaily.title: The Rise of Urban Vertical Farming
passage: A

Vertical farming, the practice of growing crops in stacked layers inside controlled environments, has moved from science fiction to commercial reality in under two decades. Proponents argue that it answers three of agriculture's most pressing problems: land scarcity, water consumption and food miles.
B

Because crops are grown hydroponically — their roots bathed in nutrient-rich water rather than soil — vertical farms can use up to 95 per cent less water than conventional agriculture. Stacking growing trays also multiplies the productive area of a single urban plot many times over, and locating farms inside cities cuts the distance food travels to consumers dramatically.
C

Critics, however, point to the industry's Achilles' heel: energy. Replacing sunlight with LED lighting is expensive, and unless the electricity comes from renewable sources, the carbon footprint of a lettuce grown indoors can exceed that of one trucked in from a distant field. Several high-profile start-ups have collapsed after underestimating operating costs.
D

The sector's future most likely lies in a narrower niche than early evangelists imagined: high-value, fast-growing crops such as herbs and salad leaves, grown close to dense urban markets where freshness commands a premium.
E

questions.why: Paragraph C says indoor lighting can make crops carbon intensive, so the claim of "all" is contradicted.

questions.why: "Several high-profile start-ups have collapsed."

questions.q: Most vertical farms are owned by supermarket chains.
questions.why: The passage never discusses who owns vertical farms.

questions.q: Which crops does the writer suggest suit vertical farming best?
questions.why: Paragraph D names herbs and salad leaves.

questions.why: The final paragraph names artificial lighting.

monarch.title: The Migration of Monarch Butterflies
passage: Every autumn, millions of monarch butterflies embark on one of the most remarkable journeys in the natural world. Leaving the cooling forests of southern Canada and the northern United States, they travel up to 4,000 kilometres to reach the warm mountain forests of central Mexico, where they spend the winter.

What makes the migration so extraordinary is that no single butterfly completes the round trip. The insects that fly south in the autumn are three or four generations removed from those that made the journey the previous year, yet they return to the very same groves of trees — sometimes even the same individual trees — that their ancestors used. How they achieve this has puzzled scientists for decades.

Research suggests that the butterflies rely on more than one method of navigation. They appear to use the position of the sun as a compass, correcting for the way it moves across the sky during the day with the help of an internal clock. In addition, experiments indicate that they can sense the Earth's magnetic field, which may guide them on cloudy days when the sun is hidden.

The Mexican overwintering sites themselves were unknown to scientists until relatively recently. Although local communities had long been aware of the butterflies, the location of the main colonies was only formally documented by researchers in 1975. Today these sites are protected, but the species still faces threats from habitat loss and a changing climate.

questions.evidence: No single butterfly completes the round trip.
questions.why: The text states no single butterfly completes the trip, so FALSE.
questions.whyZh: 原文说没有单只蝴蝶完成整趟，所以是 FALSE。

questions.q: Monarchs navigate using the position of the sun.
questions.evidence: they navigate using the position of the sun
questions.why: Directly supported by the passage.

questions.q: The Mexican overwintering sites were found before 1970.
questions.evidence: The overwintering sites in Mexico were located in 1975.
questions.why: 1975 is after 1970, so the statement is FALSE, not NOT GIVEN.
questions.whyZh: 1975 晚于 1970，所以是 FALSE 而非 NOT GIVEN。

0.text: Introduce the debate over animal testing and state your position that it should be banned.
bullets: - Paraphrase the topic: the use of animals in scientific research is controversial.
- Acknowledge both sides briefly (ethics vs. medical progress).
- State your position clearly: animal testing should be banned.
example: "While some argue animal research drives medical progress, this essay contends it should be prohibited."

0.text: Argue that causing animals to suffer for research is morally indefensible.
bullets: - Topic sentence: the strongest case against testing is ethical.
- Explain: animals can feel pain; inflicting harm needs strong justification.
- Use synonyms: "cruel" to "inhumane", "ban" to "prohibit".
example: cosmetic testing bans already exist across the EU and India.

0.text: Argue that reliable alternatives now make animal testing unnecessary.
bullets: - Topic sentence: technology has produced viable replacements.
- Explain: cell cultures and computer models increasingly replace animal tests.
- Add a benefit: these are often cheaper and more reproducible.
example: organ-on-a-chip models can predict drug toxicity without animals.

0.text: Restate the position and summarise the two main reasons.
bullets: - Restate: animal testing should be banned.
- Summarise the ethical objection and the availability of alternatives.
- End with a forward-looking statement.

1.text: Introduce both views and state a qualified position: allow testing only when essential.
bullets: - Paraphrase the topic and note the debate has two sides.
- State a nuanced position: permit it only for essential medical research.
example: "This essay argues that animal testing should be limited to essential medical purposes."

1.text: Acknowledge that some medical breakthroughs relied on animal research.
bullets: - Topic sentence: animal research has delivered genuine benefits.
- Explain: vaccines and treatments were developed with animal models.
- Add: strict oversight can limit unnecessary suffering.
example: polio and COVID-19 vaccines involved animal trials.

1.text: Argue that non-essential testing should be banned and alternatives used.
bullets: - Topic sentence: not all testing is justifiable.
- Explain: ban trivial uses such as cosmetics.
- Require alternatives (cell cultures, models) where possible.

1.text: Restate the qualified position and the conditions attached.
bullets: - Restate: allow testing only when essential.
- Summarise the medical case and the limits you would impose.

task1.title: Urban and rural households with internet access
task1.prompt:
The chart below shows the percentage of urban and rural households with internet access in one country in 2005, 2010, 2015 and 2020.

Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.
task1.chartTitle: Households with internet access (%), selected years
task1.chartDesc: A bar chart comparing the percentage of urban and rural households with internet access in 2005, 2010, 2015 and 2020. Urban access rises from 48% to 92%; rural access grows faster in relative terms from 21% to 77%, narrowing the gap.
keyPoints: Rural access grew from 21% to 77% over the same period
Rural access increased fastest between 2010 and 2015
The urban–rural gap narrowed from 27 to 15 percentage points
hints: Open with a one-sentence paraphrase of what the chart measures
Give an overview sentence: both rose and the gap narrowed
Quote the endpoint figures (48%→92% urban, 21%→77% rural)
Do not list every year — select the endpoints and the biggest change
Report the data objectively; do not explain causes

passage: A

The invention of writing is widely regarded as one of humanity's most transformative achievements. The earliest known writing systems emerged independently in at least three regions: Mesopotamia around 3200 BCE, Egypt shortly thereafter, and China by approximately 1200 BCE. Each system arose in response to specific administrative and social needs, though the paths they followed differed considerably.
B

In Mesopotamia, writing began as a system of accounting. Temple administrators needed to track goods — quantities of grain, numbers of livestock, and volumes of trade. The earliest tablets from Uruk contain nothing resembling literature or history; they are inventories and receipts. Over several centuries, these pictographic symbols became increasingly abstract, evolving into the wedge-shaped marks we call cuneiform. Only after the system had been in use for administrative purposes for roughly 500 years did scribes begin recording myths, laws, and diplomatic correspondence.
C

Egyptian hieroglyphs present a different developmental pattern. From their earliest appearance, hieroglyphs served both practical and ceremonial functions. Royal monuments bore inscriptions that combined record-keeping with religious and political propaganda. The Egyptians also developed cursive scripts — hieratic and later demotic — for everyday administrative use, while reserving the elaborate hieroglyphic forms for formal contexts.
D

Chinese writing followed yet another trajectory. The earliest confirmed Chinese characters appear on oracle bones used for divination during the Shang dynasty. These inscriptions record questions posed to ancestors and deities about warfare, harvests, and royal health. The system was already quite sophisticated by the time of these earliest surviving examples, suggesting an earlier developmental phase that has not been preserved.
E

What these three traditions share is a common pattern: writing systems tend to begin with narrow, specialized uses before expanding to serve broader communicative purposes. The technology of writing, once invented, proved remarkably adaptable, eventually transforming not just administration but human thought itself.

questions.q: According to the passage, what was the primary initial purpose of writing in Mesopotamia?
How did Egyptian hieroglyphs differ from early Mesopotamian writing?
opts: They were used exclusively for trade.
They served both practical and ceremonial purposes from the start.
They were simpler and easier to learn.
They were only used by common people.
questions.a: They served both practical and ceremonial purposes from the start.

questions.q: What does the passage suggest about the earliest Chinese writing?
opts: It was borrowed from Mesopotamian cuneiform.
It was primarily used for poetry.
It likely had an earlier stage that did not survive.
It was simpler than Egyptian hieroglyphs.
questions.a: It likely had an earlier stage that did not survive.

questions.q: Which of the following best summarizes the main argument of the passage?
opts: Writing was invented only once and spread globally.
Different writing systems emerged independently but share a pattern of expanding from narrow to broad use.
Chinese writing is older than previously believed.
Administrative needs are less important than religious ones.
questions.a: Different writing systems emerged independently but share a pattern of expanding from narrow to broad use.
